procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 26, 1965, of the Punjab High Court, Circuit Bench at Delhi in Criminal Revision No. 266-D of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Punjab High Court, Circuit Bench at Delhi, heard the case as Criminal Revision No. 266-D of 1964.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants, who were acting on behalf of the tenant, were in lawful possession of the disputed field at the time of the incident.

facts.fact: A man named Jamuna had been the tenant in possession of the disputed field for over thirty years.
The field, which was evacuee property, was sold by the government to a new owner (PW 17) and a sale certificate was issued on February 8, 1962.
On June 22, 1962, a managing officer (PW 5) issued a warrant for the delivery of the field to the new owner, and a purported delivery took place.
Jamuna's tenancy was never legally terminated.
On July 1, 1962, the new owner's party came to the field with a tractor to take forcible possession, at which point the appellants (Jamuna's relatives) confronted them.

law.law: Once the government sells an evacuee property and issues a sale certificate, it no longer has any interest in the property, and its managing officers lose the authority to deal with it.
A tenant cannot be evicted from their holding unless their tenancy is terminated and the eviction is done through a court of competent jurisdiction.
An act or order made without legal authority is considered legally non-existent ('non-est') and has no legal force or effect.

application.application: The Court determined that after the sale certificate was issued on February 8, 1962, the managing officer had no legal authority over the property.
Consequently, the warrant for delivery issued by the managing officer on June 22, 1962, was unauthorized and without legal force.
Because the delivery order was legally void, the Court found that the purported delivery of possession to the new owner never actually happened in the eyes of the law. It was a 'non-est' event.
Since Jamuna's tenancy was never terminated and the attempt to dispossess him was legally invalid, his pre-existing lawful possession of the field continued uninterrupted.
The Court viewed the new owner's actions on July 1 as an attempt to trespass and take forcible possession, not the actions of someone already in settled possession.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellants, acting on behalf of the tenant Jamuna, were in lawful possession of the field. The Court reasoned that the alleged delivery of possession to the new owner was legally void and of no effect because the government officer who ordered it no longer had any authority over the property after it had been sold. Therefore, Jamuna's long-standing and unterminated tenancy meant he remained in continuous lawful possession at the time of the incident.

issue.issue_text: Whether the purported delivery of the field to the complainant party by the managing officer was valid in law.

facts: The land in question was evacuee property that was sold at a public auction to the complainant (referred to as A or PW 17) on January 2, 1961.
A sale certificate was issued to the complainant on February 8, 1962.
A man named Jamuna (J) was the tenant on the land, and his tenancy had never been terminated.
On June 22, 1962, the managing officer issued a warrant for the delivery of the field to the complainant, and a purported delivery was carried out.
law: A landlord cannot evict a tenant from their holding without first terminating the tenancy and going through a court of competent jurisdiction.

The powers of a managing officer under the Displaced Persons Act, 1954, such as issuing a warrant for delivery under Section 19(3), apply only to properties that are still under their control and part of the compensation pool.

Once a property is sold and a sale certificate is issued, the government's interest in it is alienated, and it ceases to be an evacuee property that the managing officer can control, unless a specific provision states otherwise.
application: The Court first established that Jamuna was the tenant in possession of the field before the purported delivery.

It then reasoned that by the date of the alleged delivery (June 22, 1962), the property had already been sold and the sale certificate issued. This meant the government no longer had any interest in the land.
Because the property was no longer part of the compensation pool, the managing officer had become incompetent to deal with it. He had no authority or legal power to issue a warrant for delivery.
The Court rejected the argument that the delivery was valid under Section 19(3) of the Act, stating that this provision did not apply to properties that had ceased to be evacuee properties.
The actions of the managing officer were therefore an invalid exercise of power.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the purported delivery of the field to the complainant was not valid in law. It held that the managing officer had no authority to issue a delivery warrant for a property that had already been sold and was no longer under his control. Therefore, the alleged delivery had no legal force and was considered "non-est" (non-existent), meaning Jamuna continued to be in legal possession of the field.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants had established the right of private defence of property.

facts: The appellants' relative, Jamuna, was the long-term tenant and in lawful possession of the field in question.
A prior, alleged delivery of the property to the complainant party was found by the court to be illegal, without the authority of law, and therefore of no legal effect ("non-est").
The appellants and Jamuna were unaware of this illegal delivery and were taken by surprise when the complainant party arrived with a tractor to forcibly take possession of the land.
The complainant party's entry onto the land constituted an act of criminal trespass.
law: Section 97 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) grants every person a right to defend the property of themselves or any other person against an offence like criminal trespass.
Section 99 of the IPC states this right is not available if there is time to seek protection from public authorities, and it does not permit inflicting more harm than necessary for defence.
The law does not require a person whose property is being forcibly occupied by trespassers to run away and seek the protection of authorities.
The right of private defence serves a social purpose and should be liberally construed.
application: The Court first determined that because the alleged delivery of the property was illegal, Jamuna remained in lawful possession.
Therefore, the complainant party's act of entering the field with a tractor to level it was an act of criminal trespass, which triggered the appellants' right of private defence under Section 97.

The Court rejected the argument that the appellants should have sought help from authorities. It reasoned that the appellants were taken by surprise by the "invasion" of the field, and the law does not compel a person to flee in the face of such a peril.

The Court found that the appellants used force to prevent the complainant's party from forcibly taking the land, and on the basis of the proved facts, it could not be said that they had inflicted more harm than was necessary for the purpose of defence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellants had successfully established their right of private defence of property and had not exceeded that right, as they were lawfully defending property in their possession against an act of criminal trespass and were justified in using force to do so.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants exceeded their right of private defence.

facts: The complainant's party went to a field with a tractor to level the land, which the appellants considered to be in their possession.
The appellants attacked the complainant's party to prevent them from taking forcible possession of the land.
The appellants claimed they were taken by surprise by the 'invasion' of the field and used 'minimum force' to throw the trespassers out.
law: Section 99 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) states that the right of private defence does not extend to inflicting more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence.

The court cited a precedent (*Jai Dev v. State of Punjab*) establishing that the violence used in private defence must not be 'unduly disproportionate to the injury which is to be averted' and should not exceed its legitimate purpose.
The law does not require a person whose property is being forcibly occupied by trespassers to run away and seek the protection of the authorities, especially when taken by surprise.
A person in rightful possession is entitled to use force warranted by the situation to turn a trespasser out of the land.
application: The Court rejected the prosecution's argument that the appellants had time to seek help from public authorities, finding instead that they were 'naturally taken by surprise' by the complainant's party invading the field.
The Court noted that the appellants' position was that they used 'minimum force' to repel the trespassers.
Applying the principle that the right of private defence should be 'liberally construed', the court found that the appellants were entitled to resist the attack on their property.
The court determined that the force used by the appellants was not disproportionate to the threat of being forcibly dispossessed of their land.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that, based on the proved facts, the appellants had not inflicted more harm than was necessary for the purpose of defending their property. Therefore, it could not be said that they had exceeded their right of private defence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants, who were acting on behalf of the tenant, were in lawful possession of the disputed field at the time of the incident.
appellant_arguments: Their relation, J, was the tenant of the land for over 30 years and his tenancy was never terminated.
The alleged delivery of possession on June 22, 1962, was without the authority of law and had no effect.
The fact that some formalities were followed for an unauthorized delivery order does not mean that possession had legally passed to the complainant.
As the delivery was invalid, J continued to be in lawful possession of the property on the date of the incident, July 1, 1962.
respondent_arguments: The complainant party had taken possession of the property on June 22, 1962, following a delivery effected by the managing officer.
Whether the delivery was right or wrong, possession had been taken, and the tenant's only recourse was to agitate the matter in a court of law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the purported delivery of the field to the complainant party by the managing officer was valid in law.
appellant_arguments: The alleged delivery had no legal force and was without the authority of law.
After the sale certificate was issued to the complainant, the government no longer had any interest in the land.
Consequently, the managing officer was not competent to evict the tenant, J, or issue a warrant for the delivery of the field.
respondent_arguments: The delivery of the field was validly effected under section 19 of the Displaced Persons Act, 1954.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants had established the right of private defence of property.
appellant_arguments: Even though the plea of private defence was not taken in their statement under s. 342 Cr.P.C., the basis for it was laid in cross-examination and defence evidence.
It is well-settled that a court can consider a plea of self-defence if it arises from the material on record, even if not explicitly pleaded by the accused.
Since the tenant J was in lawful possession, the appellants had the right to defend the property against the complainant's party who were trespassing.
respondent_arguments: The appellants had no right to take the law into their own hands.
Since possession had already been delivered to the complainant's party, the tenant's only remedy was to go to a court of law, not to use force.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants exceeded their right of private defence.
appellant_arguments: The appellants used only the minimum force necessary to prevent the complainant's party from taking forcible possession of the land.
They first pushed the trespassers and then used minimum force to throw them out of the field.
Based on the facts, it cannot be said that the right of private defence was exceeded.
respondent_arguments: The appellants' actions constituted criminal offenses under ss. 447, 324 read with 149 and 148 I.P.C., as they attacked the complainant's party and caused injuries, which implies the force used was excessive and unlawful.

cases.principle: If a true owner who has been dispossessed of his property comes again to dispossess his opponents by force, then he and his associates would be members of an unlawful assembly.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A trespasser is entitled to defend their possession against the rightful owner only if they are in settled possession of the land. Stray or intermittent acts of trespass do not grant such a right against the true owner. Formalities conducted pursuant to an unauthorized order are not sufficient to establish settled possession.
obiter: If a person who has been evicted by a lawful process later returns to dispossess the rightful occupants, they and their associates would be members of an unlawful assembly.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellants, who were acting on behalf of the lawful tenant, were entitled to the right of private defence of property. The purported delivery of the field to the complainant party was based on an unauthorized order and was legally ineffective, meaning the tenant remained in lawful possession. The complainant's party, in attempting to take the field by force, were criminal trespassers and an unlawful assembly. The appellants were taken by surprise and therefore had no time to seek protection from public authorities. As they used only the minimum force necessary to repel the trespassers, they did not exceed their right of private defence and must be acquitted.
legal_tests_applied: The right of private defence of property under Section 97 IPC is available against any act which is an offence falling under the definition of criminal trespass.
The right of private defence is not available in cases where there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities, as per Section 99 IPC.
The right of private defence does not extend to inflicting more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence, as per Section 99 IPC.
A plea of self-defence can be considered by the court if it arises from the material on record, even if not explicitly pleaded by the accused in their statement under s. 342 Cr.P.C.
The burden of establishing a plea of self-defence is on the accused, who can discharge it by showing a preponderance of probabilities in their favour based on the material on record.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's argument that possession had passed to the complainant, rightly or wrongly, was rejected. The court held that formalities followed in pursuance of an 'unauthorised delivery order' were not a ground for holding that possession had legally passed.

The respondent's contention that the appellants should have agitated the matter in a court of law instead of taking the law into their own hands was rejected because the tenant was found to be in continuous lawful possession, which they had a right to defend.

The respondent's argument that the appellants had time to seek protection from public authorities was rejected. The court found that the appellants were unaware of the alleged prior delivery and were taken by surprise when the complainant party invaded the field.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the tenant remained in lawful possession of the property because the purported delivery to the complainant was unauthorized and had no legal effect.
The court characterized the complainant's party as being guilty of criminal trespass and constituting an unlawful assembly when they went to the field to intimidate the tenant and assert possession.
Because the complainant's party were criminal trespassers, the court found that the appellants were entitled under Section 97 IPC to prevent them from taking possession by using necessary force.
The court concluded on the basis of the proved facts that the appellants had used only 'minimum force to throw them out of the field' and therefore had not exceeded their right of private defence.
policy_considerations: The law does not require a person whose property is forcibly being occupied by trespassers to run away and seek the protection of the authorities.
The right of private defence serves a social purpose and should be liberally construed, as it acts as a restraining influence on bad characters and encourages the right spirit in a free citizen.
The court noted that 'There is nothing more degrading to the human spirit than to run away in the face of peril.'
